title: Modular Arithmetic
description: Arithmetic that wraps around a modulus, the key to avoiding overflow in maths problems

blocks.text: Modular arithmetic is arithmetic that wraps around, like a clock. It is one of the most important tools in competitive programming, because it lets us work with enormous numbers without ever overflowing.
Almost every counting problem that asks for the answer modulo 10^9 plus 7 is really asking you to do modular arithmetic correctly.
Think of a 12 hour clock. Four hours after 11 o clock is not 15, it is 3, because the hours wrap around after 12. That wrapping is exactly modular arithmetic.

blocks.caption: On a clock, values wrap around once they reach the modulus

blocks.text: The result of a mod m is the remainder when a is divided by m, and it always lands in the range 0 to m minus 1. We say two numbers are congruent modulo m if they leave the same remainder.
Most languages use the percent sign for modulo. There is one trap: in C++, Java, and JavaScript, the result of the percent operator can be negative when the left side is negative.
To force a value into the proper range 0 to m minus 1, add m and take the modulo again. Python already returns a non negative result, so it does not need this fix.

codes.python:
def mod(a, m):
    return a % m                 # Python already returns a non-negative result

content.title: 3. Rules for Add, Subtract, and Multiply

blocks.text: The magic of modular arithmetic is that you can take the modulo at every step and still get the right final answer. This is what keeps numbers small.

blocks.caption: You may reduce each operand modulo m before combining them
blocks.alt: Rules for Add, Subtract, and Multiply

items: Addition: (a + b) mod m equals ((a mod m) + (b mod m)) mod m
Subtraction: add m before the final mod so the result never goes negative
Multiplication: (a times b) mod m equals ((a mod m) times (b mod m)) mod m
Division does not work this way; it needs a modular inverse

codes.python:
def add_mod(a, b, m): return (a % m + b % m) % m
def sub_mod(a, b, m): return (a % m - b % m + m) % m
def mul_mod(a, b, m): return (a % m) * (b % m) % m

blocks.text: You will see the number 10^9 plus 7 everywhere. Problems ask for answers modulo this value so the result fits in a normal 32 or 64 bit integer, even when the true count is astronomically large.
It is chosen because it is a large prime just under a round power of ten. Being prime is important, because it guarantees modular division works through a modular inverse.

Watch for overflow:

Even under a mod, multiplying two numbers near 10^9 gives about 10^18. Use a 64 bit type in C++ and Java, and BigInt in JavaScript, before taking the mod.
Dividing under a modulus is not as simple as dividing the remainders. To divide by a number, you multiply by its modular inverse, the value that acts like its reciprocal in modular arithmetic.
When the modulus is prime, the inverse of a is a raised to the power m minus 2, computed with fast exponentiation. That connection is why primality of the modulus matters.
It appears anywhere answers get huge or wrap around.

items: Counting problems that report the answer modulo a large prime
Hashing, where values are kept inside a fixed range
Cyclic structures like clocks, calendars, and ring buffers
Combinatorics with factorials and binomial coefficients

blocks.text: Whenever you see modulo 10^9 plus 7, remember to reduce at every step, not just at the end.
